title: Tuple to Association - Turning Sequences into Lookup Tables
narrative:
A `Tuple` is an ordered sequence of items, whereas an `Association`
    is a mapping from keys to values. Turning the former into the latter
    is one of the most common things you do when modelling data:
    you have a list of value objects, and you want to look them up
    by one of their fields.

    The `Tuple` type offers three flavours of this conversion,
    one for every kind of `Association` that exists in Sprouts:

    - `toAssociation(Class, Function, Class, Function)` creates an
      unordered association, the fastest of the three.
    - `toLinkedAssociation(Class, Function, Class, Function)` creates
      an association which preserves the order of the tuple.
    - `toSortedAssociation(Class, Function, Class, Function, Comparator)`
      creates an association whose entries are ordered by their keys,
      with a natural order variant for keys which are `Comparable`.

    Note how every mapper function is preceded by the type of the
    objects it produces. This is because an `Association` always tracks
    the types of its keys and values, and a lambda, unlike a tuple,
    cannot tell us what it produces.

    All of these conversions are exact shorthands for filling an
    initially empty association with the derived key-value pairs,
    one after another. So if two items produce the same key,
    then the last one wins.

    When you do not want to lose the other ones, then reach for the
    grouping conversions instead, which exist in the same three
    flavours and collect all the values of a key into a `Tuple`:

    - `toGroupedAssociation(Class, Function, Class, Function)`
    - `toGroupedLinkedAssociation(Class, Function, Class, Function)`
    - `toGroupedSortedAssociation(Class, Function, Class, Function, Comparator)`

    These are lossless: every single item of the tuple ends up in
    exactly one of the groups of the resulting association.

features.id: A tuple of value objects can be turned into a lookup table.

extraInfo:
This is the bread and butter use case of the `toAssociation` method:
            you have a tuple of value objects and you want to look them up
            by one of their fields.

            The two mapper functions define what becomes the key and what
            becomes the value of every entry, and each of them is preceded
            by the type of the objects it produces.

blocks.text: A tuple of documentaries, each with a title and a runtime.
We index the runtimes of the documentaries by their titles.
We can now look up the runtime of a documentary by its title.
The association knows the types we declared for its keys and values.
It holds exactly one entry per item of the tuple.
Being a plain association, it is neither linked nor sorted.

features.id: The three kinds of conversion produce the three kinds of association.

extraInfo:
Sprouts knows three kinds of associations: plain (unordered),
            linked (ordered by insertion) and sorted (ordered by key).
            There is one conversion method for each of them, and they all
            report their kind through `isLinked()` and `isSorted()`.

blocks.text: A tuple of words we want to index by their length.
We convert the tuple in all three ways.
code: var plain  = words.toAssociation(       Integer.class, { it.length() }, String.class, { it })
var linked = words.toLinkedAssociation( Integer.class, { it.length() }, String.class, { it })
var sorted = words.toSortedAssociation( Integer.class, { it.length() }, String.class, { it }, Comparator.naturalOrder())

blocks.text: Each of them reports the kind of association it is.
They all hold the same entries, they merely differ in their order.

features.id: A linked association preserves the order of the tuple it came from.

extraInfo:
The `toLinkedAssociation` method is the one to reach for when
            the order of your tuple carries meaning. Iterating over the
            resulting association yields the entries in exactly the order
            in which the items they came from appear in the tuple.

blocks.text: A tuple of documentaries in no particular order.
We index them by their titles, using a linked association.
The keys appear in the very order of the tuple.
And so do the values.
We reverse the tuple and convert it again.
The order of the entries is reversed as well.
Both associations still hold the same entries, which is why they are equal.

features.id: A sorted association orders its entries by their keys, not by the tuple.

extraInfo:
The `toSortedAssociation` method takes a `Comparator` as its
            last parameter, which defines the order of the keys in the
            resulting association. The order of the tuple is irrelevant
            for the resulting order, it only decides which value wins
            if two items produce the same key.

blocks.text: A tuple of documentaries in no particular order.
We index them by their titles, sorted alphabetically.
The keys are sorted, irrespective of the order of the tuple.
The association reports itself as sorted.
We do the same, but with a reversed comparator.
The keys are sorted the other way around.

features.id: The natural order variant of `toSortedAssociation` needs no comparator.

extraInfo:
Sorting by the natural order of the keys is so common that
            there is a variant of `toSortedAssociation` without a comparator.
            It requires the key type to implement `Comparable` and is
            exactly equivalent to passing `Comparator.naturalOrder()`.

blocks.text: A tuple of documentaries.
We convert it without supplying a comparator...
...and once more, with the natural order comparator.
Both produce the very same sorted association.

features.id: Converting an empty tuple yields an empty association of the declared types.

extraInfo:
An empty tuple is a perfectly valid input for all of these
            conversions. Because the key and value types are declared
            explicitly, the resulting association knows its types even
            though there was not a single item to derive them from.

blocks.text: An empty tuple of documentaries.
We convert it in all four ways.
code: var plain   = empty.toAssociation(       String.class, { it.title() }, Integer.class, { it.minutes() })
var linked  = empty.toLinkedAssociation( String.class, { it.title() }, Integer.class, { it.minutes() })
var sorted  = empty.toSortedAssociation( String.class, { it.title() }, Integer.class, { it.minutes() }, Comparator.naturalOrder())
var natural = empty.toSortedAssociation( String.class, { it.title() }, Integer.class, { it.minutes() })

blocks.text: All of them are empty.
All of them know the types we declared.
code: [plain, linked, sorted, natural].every { it.keyType() == String && it.valueType() == Integer }

blocks.text: And all of them are of the kind we asked for.
They are equal to the empty associations of the corresponding factory methods.

features.id: When two items produce the same key, then the last one wins.

extraInfo:
An association cannot hold duplicate keys, so something has to
            give when two items of a tuple produce the same key.
            These conversion methods are exact shorthands for putting all
            derived pairs into an empty association one after another,
            which means the value of the **last** of the colliding items wins.

blocks.text: A tuple of words, where several of them start with the same letter.
We index the words by their first character.
Only one entry per distinct first character survives, the last one of each.

features.id: A colliding key keeps the position of the first item, but the value of the last.

extraInfo:
In a linked association the position of an entry is decided when
            the key is first inserted, and putting a new value for an existing
            key does not move it. This is the behaviour of a `LinkedHashMap`,
            and since these conversions are shorthands for repeated `put` calls,
            it is the behaviour you get here as well.

blocks.text: A tuple whose first and second item share their first character.
We index the words by their first character, preserving the order.
The 'a' entry sits at the position of "apple", the first of the two...
...but it holds the value derived from "avocado", the last of the two.

features.id: A comparator which is inconsistent with equals is handed straight to the association.

extraInfo:
Just like a `SortedMap`, a sorted `Association` wants a comparator
            which is consistent with `equals`, because it tells its keys apart
            through their equality, while it positions them through the comparator.

            This conversion does not invent a policy of its own for such a
            comparator. Whatever the sorted association makes of it is exactly
            what you get, because the conversion is nothing but a shorthand for
            putting the derived pairs into that very association.

blocks.text: A tuple of words which differ only in their casing, and a comparator ignoring casing.
We convert the tuple using that comparator...
...and then assemble the very same association by hand.
The two are indistinguishable, down to their size and iteration order.
We convert the very same tuple using the natural order, which is consistent with equals.
Every distinct word became an entry of its own, sorted naturally.

features.id: The conversions are exact shorthands for filling an empty association.

extraInfo:
The contract of these conversion methods is defined in terms of
            the association factory methods you already know: create an empty
            association of the desired kind, and then put all derived
            key-value pairs into it, in the order of the tuple.
            This specification verifies that promise directly.

blocks.text: A tuple with a couple of duplicate keys hidden in it.
We build the three associations by hand, using plain `put` calls.
And then again, using the conversion methods.
code: var plain  = words.toAssociation(       Character.class, keyOf, String.class, valueOf)
var linked = words.toLinkedAssociation( Character.class, keyOf, String.class, valueOf)
var sorted = words.toSortedAssociation( Character.class, keyOf, String.class, valueOf, Comparator.naturalOrder())

blocks.text: The results are indistinguishable, down to their iteration order.

features.id: Both mappers are applied exactly once per item, in the order of the tuple.

extraInfo:
The items of a tuple are processed from the first to the last,
            and each of the two mapper functions sees every item exactly once.
            This holds even for items whose keys end up colliding, because
            the value of a later item can only win if it was computed.

blocks.text: A tuple with a duplicate key hidden in it, and two recording mappers.
We convert the tuple into an association.
Every item was passed to both mappers exactly once, in the order of the tuple.
The resulting association has the expected entries.

features.id: A mapper producing null is an error, because associations cannot hold nulls. [0]

extraInfo:
A `Tuple` may hold null items, but an `Association` may hold
            neither null keys nor null values. So when one of the two mappers
            produces a null, the conversion fails with a `NullPointerException`
            which tells you exactly which item is to blame.

blocks.text: We perform a conversion whose mapper produces a null.
A null pointer exception is thrown...
...naming the offending item, its index and what went wrong.
We check this for the key mapper and the value mapper of every conversion.

conversion: { Tuple.of("a","bb").toAssociation(String, { it == "bb" ? null : it }, Integer, { it.length() }) }
{ Tuple.of("a","bb").toAssociation(String, { it }, Integer, { it == "bb" ? null : it.length() }) }
{ Tuple.of("a","bb").toSortedAssociation(String, { it == "bb" ? null : it }, Integer, { it.length() }, Comparator.naturalOrder()) }
{ Tuple.of("a","bb").toSortedAssociation(String, { it }, Integer, { it == "bb" ? null : it.length() }, Comparator.naturalOrder()) }

features.id: The declared types are enforced by the resulting association.

extraInfo:
Types are tracked in this library, which is why you have to
            declare the key and value types of the association you want.
            If a mapper produces something which does not fit the type
            it was paired with, then the association rejects it.
            (In statically typed Java code the compiler catches this for you,
            here we have to sneak past it using dynamic Groovy.)

blocks.text: We claim to produce integer keys, but produce strings.
The association rejects the key.
We claim to produce integer values, but produce strings.
The association rejects the value.

features.id: Converting a tuple never modifies the tuple itself.

extraInfo:
A `Tuple` is an immutable value object, so turning it into an
            association is a pure read of its items. This is a fundamental
            contract we verify here by comparing the tuple with a snapshot
            taken before the conversions.

blocks.text: A tuple and a snapshot of its contents.
We convert the tuple in all four ways.
code: docs.toSortedAssociation( String.class, { it.title() }, Integer.class, { it.minutes() }, Comparator.naturalOrder())

blocks.text: The tuple is completely unaffected.

features.id: A large tuple, grown through many insertions, converts to a complete association.

extraInfo:
A `Tuple` is backed by a tree of arrays whose shape depends on how
            the tuple was built. This specification grows a large tuple through
            many insertions at random positions, so that the resulting tree is
            deep and irregular, and then verifies that every single item of it
            makes it into the resulting associations.

blocks.text: A large tuple, grown through insertions at random positions.
The tuple matches the reference list before we start.
We index every number by itself.
code: var plain  = tuple.toAssociation(       Integer.class, { it }, String.class, { "#" + it })
var linked = tuple.toLinkedAssociation( Integer.class, { it }, String.class, { "#" + it })
var sorted = tuple.toSortedAssociation( Integer.class, { it }, String.class, { "#" + it })

blocks.text: All of them hold every single number of the tuple.
Every number can be looked up in every one of them.
The linked association preserved the order of the tuple...
...while the sorted association ordered the numbers naturally.

features.id: An exception thrown by a mapper is relayed to the caller.

extraInfo:
The mapper functions are your code, so if one of them fails,
            then the conversion fails with it. Nothing is swallowed,
            and no half-built association is handed back to you.

blocks.text: A tuple of words and a mapper which trips over the second one.
We convert the tuple with that failing mapper.
code: String.class,  { it == "boom" ? { throw new IllegalStateException("Boom!") }() : it },

blocks.text: The exception of the mapper reaches us unchanged.

features.id: A tuple of value objects can be grouped into an association of tuples.

extraInfo:
Where `toAssociation` builds a lookup table with a single value per key,
            `toGroupedAssociation` builds one with a whole `Tuple` of values per key.
            Every item of the tuple ends up in exactly one of those groups.

            The two mapper functions play the same roles as before, except that the
            second one no longer produces the value of an entry, but a single member
            of a group.

blocks.text: A tuple of documentaries, some of which share their topic.
We group the titles of the documentaries by their topic.
Every topic is associated with a tuple of all the titles which share it.
There is one entry per distinct topic, not one per documentary.
The association knows the type of its keys, and that its values are tuples.
Being a plain association, it is neither linked nor sorted.

features.id: Grouping is lossless, whereas the plain conversion keeps only the last value.

extraInfo:
This is the whole point of the grouping conversions. An `Association` cannot
            hold two values under one key, so `toAssociation` has to drop all but the last
            of them. `toGroupedAssociation` instead widens the values into tuples, which
            means that nothing of the original tuple is lost.

blocks.text: A tuple of words, several of which start with the same letter.
We convert it in both ways, using the very same two mappers.
Both associations have one entry per distinct first character.
The collapsed one silently forgot "apple" and "banana".
The grouped one kept every single word.
Which we can also confirm by counting all the grouped words.

features.id: The three kinds of grouped conversion produce the three kinds of association.

extraInfo:
Just like the plain conversions, the grouping conversions come in three
            flavours, one for every kind of `Association` in Sprouts.

blocks.text: A tuple of words we want to group by their length.
We group the tuple in all three ways.
code: var plain  = words.toGroupedAssociation(       Integer.class, { it.length() }, String.class, { it })
var linked = words.toGroupedLinkedAssociation( Integer.class, { it.length() }, String.class, { it })
var sorted = words.toGroupedSortedAssociation( Integer.class, { it.length() }, String.class, { it }, Comparator.naturalOrder())

blocks.text: Each of them reports the kind of association it is.
They all hold the same groups, they merely differ in their order.

features.id: A grouped linked association keeps the order in which the keys first occur.

extraInfo:
A group takes its position from the first item which produced its key,
            because that is when the key entered the association. The items which
            join the group later do not move it.

blocks.text: A tuple of documentaries whose topics are interleaved.
We group the titles by their topic, preserving the order.
The groups appear in the order in which their topics first occur.
And within every group, the titles appear in the order of the tuple.

features.id: A grouped sorted association orders its groups by their keys.

extraInfo:
The `toGroupedSortedAssociation` method takes a `Comparator` as its last
            parameter, which orders the groups by their keys. The order of the tuple
            still decides the order of the values inside every group.

blocks.text: A tuple of documentaries whose topics are interleaved.
We group the titles by topic, sorted alphabetically.
The groups are ordered by their topics, irrespective of the tuple.
But the titles inside the groups still follow the order of the tuple.
We do the same, but with a reversed comparator.
The groups are ordered the other way around.
While the contents of the groups are untouched.

features.id: The natural order variant of `toGroupedSortedAssociation` needs no comparator.

extraInfo:
Just like for the plain conversions, sorting the groups by the natural
            order of their keys does not require you to pass a comparator, as long
            as the key type implements `Comparable`.

blocks.text: A tuple of documentaries.
We group them without supplying a comparator...
...and once more, with the natural order comparator.
Both produce the very same sorted association of groups.

features.id: The values of a grouped association are tuples, which is what its value type says.

extraInfo:
This is the one thing to keep in mind about the grouping conversions:
            the type you pair with the value mapper is the type of the items
            **inside** the value tuples, not the value type of the association.
            The association itself holds tuples, and says so.

blocks.text: A tuple of words.
We group the words by their length, declaring `String` as the value item type.
The value type of the association is `Tuple`, not `String`.
And the tuples it holds are tuples of strings.
Those tuples do not allow null items.

features.id: A key produced by a single item is associated with a group of size one.

extraInfo:
There is no special case for keys which only a single item produced.
            They are associated with a tuple like every other key, one holding
            exactly one value. This keeps the shape of the result predictable.

blocks.text: A tuple of words which all have a different first character.
We group them by their first character.
Every group is a tuple of exactly one word.

features.id: Equal values within a group are kept rather than merged.

extraInfo:
A group is a `Tuple`, not a `ValueSet`, which means that it holds
            duplicates. So if two items of the tuple produce both the same key
            and the same value, then that value appears twice in the group.

blocks.text: A tuple in which one word occurs twice.
We group the words by their first character.
Both occurrences of the repeated word are in the group.

features.id: Grouping an empty tuple yields an empty association of the declared types.

extraInfo:
An empty tuple has no items to group, so the result is an empty
            association. It still knows its key type, and that its values

features.id: A large tuple is grouped into buckets which hold every single item.

extraInfo:
This specification grows a large tuple through many insertions at random
            positions, so that the tree behind it is deep and irregular, and then
            groups it into buckets. Not a single item may go missing on the way.

blocks.text: A large tuple, grown through insertions at random positions.
We group the numbers into ten buckets, by their last digit.
There are ten buckets, sorted by their digit.
Every bucket holds a hundred numbers, all of them ending in its digit.
Taken together, the buckets hold every single number of the tuple.
And within every bucket, the numbers follow the order of the tuple.

features.id: A grouping conversion rejects a key or a group member of the wrong type.

extraInfo:
A grouping conversion tracks a key type and the item type of the groups, and
            it rejects a mapper which does not honour them. The key is checked by the
            association, whereas the members of a group are checked against the item
            type of the tuples the groups are made of.

            Because the conversion knows which item it is busy with when a group member
            turns out to be of the wrong type, it can tell you exactly where to look.
            (In statically typed Java code the compiler catches all of this for you,
            here we have to sneak past it using dynamic Groovy.)

blocks.text: We claim to produce integer keys, but produce strings.
The association rejects the key.
We claim to produce integer group members, but produce a string for the second item.
The group rejects the value...
...naming the offending item, its index and the type it actually produced.
We do the very same thing, but declare the group members as a primitive type.
The group rejects the value just as decisively, naming the primitive type.
And it points at the offending item in exactly the same way.

features.id: A group declared on a supertype accepts the subtypes of that type.

extraInfo:
The item type of a group is a bound, not an exact match: a group of `Number`
            holds an `Integer` like any other number, exactly like a `Tuple<Number>` does.

            This is worth pinning, because the check which rejects a group member of the
            wrong type has to tell a subtype apart from an unrelated type. A check which
            merely compared the two types for equality would pass every specification
            above and still turn a perfectly good `Integer` away here.

blocks.text: A tuple of words we want to group by themselves.
We collect their lengths into groups declared to hold any kind of number.
The integers were accepted into the groups of numbers.
And the groups report the supertype we declared as their item type.
We hand the very same groups a value which is no number at all.
That one is turned away, naming the type it expected.

features.id: A group can be a tuple of primitive values.

extraInfo:
The type paired with the value mapper is the item type of the value tuples,
            and a `Tuple` may be declared on a primitive item type, storing its items
            in a dense array. The conversion hands that type to the groups exactly as
            you declare it.

            Do keep in mind that a tuple tracks its item type, which means that a group
            of primitives is *not* equal to a group of the very same values boxed.
            Pick one of the two and stick with it.

            (Below we write `Integer.TYPE`, which is the very same class object as the
            `int.class` you would write in Java.)
